title: Lena's first lesson
text: Lena stood in the doorway of the gym with her sports bag clutched to her chest and a swarm of butterflies in her stomach. She had agreed to come only because her older brother, who had trained there for years, would not stop talking about it, and because she had run out of excuses. The hall smelled of rubber and old sweat. Around the large blue mat, a dozen teenagers in white jackets were stretching and laughing as if this were the most natural place in the world, and Lena felt like **a fish out of water**.

The coach, a broad man with a calm voice, did not make a speech. He simply asked everyone to stand in a line and showed them how to fall. It sounded absurd to Lena; she had come to learn how to defend herself, not to practise lying on the floor. Lena glanced at her brother, who was demonstrating a roll with infuriating ease, and decided that she would never forgive him. Yet after twenty minutes of rolling sideways and slapping the mat with her arm, she began to understand his point. 'Nobody wins a fight from the ground,' he said, 'but nobody wins at all if they are afraid of being thrown.'

Then came the partner work. Lena was paired with a girl called Marina, who was smaller than her but moved with the confidence of someone who had done this a thousand times. Within a minute Lena was on her back, staring at the ceiling lamps and wondering how it had happened. Marina offered her a hand and grinned. 'Everybody lands like that on the first day,' she said. 'It means you are doing it properly.' Lena did not feel properly anything, only very bruised, and she was grateful that the lights were too bright for anyone to notice her face.

By the end of the hour her arms were trembling and her pride was in pieces. She seriously considered throwing in the towel and telling her brother that sport was not for her, but the coach stopped her at the door. He did not ask whether she had enjoyed it. Instead he asked what she had noticed, and Lena, after a pause, said that she had noticed how quickly she had stopped thinking about everything else. He nodded as if that had been the right answer, and then he told her, without any ceremony, that the group met again on Thursday.

She went back on Thursday, mostly out of curiosity. This time she arrived early and helped carry the mats, which earned her a surprised look from her brother. The falls were less frightening, and when Marina showed her a simple throw, Lena managed it on the fourth attempt, with her partner landing softly and laughing. It was a small thing, but she walked home feeling taller, and she told nobody, because she wanted to keep the feeling to herself for a little while longer.

Weeks later, a boy at school pushed past her in the corridor and, for the first time, Lena did not feel the old wave of embarrassment. She did not use anything she had learnt; she simply stood her ground and looked at him until he apologised. Her brother, when she told him, shrugged and said that this was what the training was really about. She suspected he was right, but she also suspected that she would go on coming to the gym for much simpler reasons.

questions.q: Why did Lena go to the gym?
options: Her mother had insisted on it.
She could not find a reason to refuse.
She wanted to prove something to a rival.
The coach had personally invited her.

questions.q: What does 'It' in 'It sounded absurd to Lena' refer to?
options: The coach's calm voice.
The idea of a long speech.
The instruction to form a row.
The task of practising falls.

questions.q: 'A fish out of water' in paragraph 1 means that Lena felt …
options: uncomfortable in an unfamiliar place.
weaker than everybody else.
ready to leave at once.
too hot in the hall.

questions.q: What did the coach say about falling?
options: Fighters should avoid the floor.
Learning to fall is a waste of time.
Fear of hitting the floor spoils any fight.
Beginners must practise it every day.

questions.q: What made Lena consider giving up after the first class?
options: Her brother's laughter.
A quarrel with Marina.
Exhaustion and embarrassment.
The coach's criticism.

questions.q: Which fact is NOT mentioned in the text?
options: Lena's mother came to watch the training.
Marina encouraged Lena after her fall.
Lena helped to carry equipment.
The coach asked Lena a question at the door.

questions.q: What does the ending suggest about Lena?
options: She wishes she had never joined.
She intends to beat her brother.
She hopes to become a coach.
She has found confidence and pleasure.

discuss: Have you ever joined a club or class where you knew nobody? How did you feel?
Why do you think the coach began with falling rather than fighting?
Is there a sport or activity you would like to try but are afraid of?
